text: ← All chapters 00 · Content revision 1 The structure of Practical LLM in Rust Start from the completed Rust language model, follow the practical chapter sequence, and distinguish CPU examples, external corpus preparation and the GPU-backed path. In this chapter Understand the practical course's starting implementation, prerequisites and chapter sequence, and distinguish small examples from larger measured runs. Start from a working model This course starts from a working language model and studies what must change as the data, model and workload grow. The starting implementation is a separate copy of the model completed in LLM from scratch. It already contains byte-pair tokenization, tensors, automatic differentiation, a causal decoder, training, evaluation, checkpoints and cached generation. Here we extend those parts. Chapter 0 is an orientation. Chapter 1 begins the learning material by recording exactly what the small reference model demonstrates. That record gives later changes a concrete comparison point. Before starting Complete LLM from scratch or bring equivalent experience with Rust, byte-pair encoding, causal attention, gradients and next-token training. The first course’s Chapter 39 shows the complete small model. Familiarity with that model matters more than memorizing its chapter numbers. The initial reference and Rust loading of an already prepared corpus run on a CPU. The GPU-backed practical path requires a compatible NVIDIA GPU. The external corpus-preparation example uses NVIDIA NeMo Curator and needs a GPU and driver compatible with its pinned CUDA/RAPIDS environment. NeMo prepares text outside the Rust model; another tool can supply the same prepared-document format. Keep the completed model as the starting point The first course builds the mechanisms of a small causal language model. This course begins with its completed implementation and studies how data handling, execution, training and inference must change for larger workloads. The Rust implementation for this course lives in rust/crates/llm-from-scratch-practical. Its examples extend that copy; the first course keeps its own implementation. Follow the practical path Chapter 1: Record the reference model binds the tiny experiment to its inputs and separates repeatable results from claims about language quality or speed. Chapter 2: Prepare a corpus separates external text preparation from Rust loading, and preserves document and split identity. Chapter 3 extends byte-pair encoding. It adds bounded ingestion, local pair updates and efficient application of frozen merge ranks to the existing tokenizer. The practical course index links to the lessons currently available. The later curriculum continues with variable-length batches and packing, configurable decoder depth and shape, GPU execution, larger training runs, complete resume state, evaluation, adaptation, quantized inference and serving. These are stages of one causal text model. Their examples become available as each mechanism is implemented and measured. Read the examples at their stated scale Small fixtures make intermediate values inspectable: a pair count, a token sequence, a loss or a restored state. They establish the behavior shown for those inputs. They do not establish full-corpus throughput, useful generated language, or a larger model’s memory use. Full-data runs and hardware measurements supply that separate evidence. Use the sequence to navigate An ordered chapter list connects each available lesson to its purpose and names the later stages. The individual lessons introduce diagrams where a computation or comparison benefits from one. Continue with the reference experiment Corpus preparation and tokenization supply the causal decoder’s inputs. Later chapters change how that same model is configured, trained, evaluated and used for generation. Start by establishing the reference experiment in Chapter 1. Quick reference The fixed scalar reference Terms for interpreting the tiny decoder's input identity, regression evidence, replay and checkpoint limits. Overlapping windows can score the same within-document transition occurrence repeatedly; this reference scores 1,744 slots representing 442 occurrences. The problem: changes need a fixed comparison point The final chapter of LLM from scratch joined the tokenizer, decoder, training, evaluation, checkpoint and generation code. This practical course starts from a separate copy of that implementation. If the data, configuration and code change together, a changed result no longer tells you which version you observed. You need a fixed reference that identifies its inputs and states exactly what its checks establish. This chapter runs the completed first-course pipeline without modifying it. The practical copy can then evolve while this comparison point stays fixed. The example gives that reference an input identity and a report whose claims stay attached to their evidence. The identity identifies the fixed inputs. The checks establish which behavior this execution reproduced. Neither establishes useful laptop-scale capability. What the reference actually does The fixture assigns 8 documents to training, 2 to validation and 2 to test. The decoder has 1188 learned scalar parameters and context capacity 4 tokens. Its primary training schedule and separately executed replay each perform 32 updates on full batches of 16 windows, with 4 valid targets per window. Therefore, each schedule consumes 32\cdot16\cdot4=2048 valid training targets. One pipeline invocation includes both schedules: 4096 targets altogether. These counts are derived from the frozen full-batch schedule, not from a new runtime token counter. Evaluation targets and generated tokens are separate quantities. The report’s independent_schedules field counts two separately executed copies of the same schedule from training seed 39, not statistically independent seed samples. The replay agrees bit for bit with the primary training result in this execution. The selected decoder and frozen bigram then score the same 1744 overlapping test-window target slots. Their mean negative log-likelihoods are approximately 3.866087547 and 3.981342714 nats per slot, respectively. This known comparison is a regression check: rerunning it can expose changes in the checked behavior. It is not an independent estimate of generalization. There are only 442 within-document transition occurrences in those test documents. Overlapping windows repeat occurrences, so 1744 is not a count of distinct transitions. A separate policy would score each occurrence once, using the longest available causal prefix capped at four tokens and only its newest-position distribution. This run does not report numeric mean NLL or perplexity under that policy. The checkpoint round trip preserves its encoded bytes, model and optimizer bits, and tokenizer. The restored decoder reproduces logits for the fixed At probe, encoded as token IDs [67,118]. Cached and complete-prefix generation agree on token IDs [260,34,34]: Cyrillic т followed by two spaces. Agreement checks the two generation paths; those three tokens do not demonstrate useful language quality. The solution: identify inputs, then interpret evidence R_{\mathrm{ref}}=\operatorname{SHA256}(\mathrm{config}_{1188}\Vert\mathrm{fixture}\Vert\mathrm{source\_revision}) The identity’s symbols and fixed settings R_{\mathrm{ref}} is a 256-bit digest, displayed as 64 lowercase hexadecimal characters. Its three named inputs are: \mathrm{config}_{1188}: a canonical record of eighteen tiny-run settings, together with the invariant that the decoder has 1188 parameters. \mathrm{fixture}: a canonical record of SHA-256 digests of the exact corpus bytes and exact split-manifest bytes. Even a byte change that leaves parsed JSON meaning unchanged creates a different input identity. \mathrm{source\_revision}: a verified source identity combining a baseline revision with the exact forty Rust source files of the completed first-course crate, including its module declarations in lib.rs. Here \Vert means composition into the shared identity format’s named, canonical fields, not writing three unframed strings beside one another. That distinction matters: without field boundaries, different input sequences can have the same concatenated bytes. The helper orders fields, serializes one unambiguous record and hashes its complete bytes. The settings fix eight BPE merges; decoder width, feed-forward width and context capacity of four; one attention head and one block; stride one; training and evaluation batch sizes of sixteen and one hundred twenty-eight; thirty-two updates; learning rate 0.04; gradient-norm cap 1; training seed 39; generation seed 38; bigram smoothing 1; generation temperature 0.8; top-k four; and three generated tokens. let fields = [ ("parameters", "1188".to_owned()), ("bpe_merges", config.bpe_merges().to_string()), ("model_width", config.model_width().to_string()), ("heads", config.heads().to_string()), ( "feed_forward_width", config.feed_forward_width().to_string(), ), ("layers", config.layers().to_string()), ("context_length", config.context_length().to_string()), ("window_stride", config.window_stride().to_string()), ("update_batch_size", config.update_batch_size().to_string()), ( "evaluation_batch_size", config.evaluation_batch_size().to_string(), ), ("updates", config.updates().to_string()), ( "learning_rate_f64_bits", format!("{:016x}", config.learning_rate().to_bits()), ), ( "max_gradient_norm_f64_bits", format!("{:016x}", config.max_gradient_norm().to_bits()), ), ("seed", config.seed().to_string()), ("generation_seed", config.generation_seed().to_string()), ( "bigram_alpha_f64_bits", format!("{:016x}", config.bigram_alpha().to_bits()), ), ( "generation_temperature_f64_bits", format!("{:016x}", config.generation_temperature().to_bits()), ), ("generation_top_k", config.generation_top_k().to_string()), ("generation_tokens", config.generation_tokens().to_string()), ]; It then rejects changed corpus or split bytes before training or checkpoint work. Only accepted fixed inputs reach the existing pipeline. The wrapper calls that pipeline once; the pipeline itself performs primary training and replay. } if sha256(split_source.as_bytes()).as_hex() != SPLITS_SHA256 { return Err(ReferenceHandoffError::FixtureMismatch("split manifest")); } // Safe callers obtain this opaque proof only through the foundation's // approved-manifest/compiled-census verification, not a revision string. let identity = reference_input_identity( &tiny_config_identity()?, corpus_source.as_bytes(), split_source.as_bytes(), source.identity(), )?; let digest = identity.digest()?; let observation = run_capstone( corpus_source, split_source, checkpoint_path, CapstoneConfig::tiny(), )?; let evaluation = observation.final_evaluation(); let checkpoint = observation.checkpoint(); if observation.training().parameter_count() != 1188 || observation.training().optimizer_step() != 32 || !observation.training().replay_bitwise() || evaluation.window_count() != 436 || evaluation.window_target_slot_count() != 1744 || evaluation.document_transition_occurrence_count() != 442 || !evaluation.decoder().mean_nll().is_finite() || !evaluation.bigram().mean_nll().is_finite() || !checkpoint.bytes_roundtrip() || !checkpoint.model_bits_exact() || !checkpoint.optimizer_bits_exact() || !checkpoint.tokenizer_exact() || !checkpoint.prompt_logits_bitwise() || !observation.generation().tokens_exact() || !observation.generation().decisions_bitwise() || !observation.generation().rng_state_exact() { return Err(ReferenceHandoffError::Invariant( "scalar reference handoff evidence changed", )); } Ok(ReferenceHandoffTrace { identity, digest, source_revision: source.source_revision().to_owned(), observation, }) } What matching identities do not prove A matching digest identifies the same canonical input record, subject to the hash’s collision-resistance assumption. It does not prove that the algorithm is correct or that a new machine will reproduce every floating-point bit. The source identity deliberately covers the forty first-course source files, not the evolving practical crate, this chapter’s reporting wrapper or interface. Toolchain, locked dependencies and arithmetic environment are recorded separately. A matching source digest is therefore not evidence that two execution environments match. The temporary checkpoint path is also outside the input identity; changing that path does not change the model’s fixed inputs. Likewise, exact checkpoint reload is narrower than complete job resumption. This check does not restore every data cursor, in-flight operation or whole-job continuation state. No laptop throughput is measured here. History: reporting conditions and measuring variation A language-model score without its input conditions and scope does not identify what was evaluated or establish which capabilities were checked. Model Cards for Model Reporting was presented in 2019. Mitchell and colleagues propose model documentation that includes intended uses and evaluation conditions; a model card is not itself proof of quality. Model Cards describe evaluation conditions and intended uses; later fine-tuning experiments study variation across initializations and data orders. Reporting scope and measuring variation answer different questions. In Fine-Tuning Pretrained Language Models: Weight Initializations, Data Orders, and Early Stopping, published in 2020, Dodge and colleagues study fine-tuning variability associated with initialization and data order for pretrained language models. This does not measure variability in the course’s tiny decoder. Keep a fixed regression reference when changing an LLM pipeline, while recording separately the evidence needed for quality, seed sensitivity and hardware claims. The Rust reporting contrast uses the same observation. Reading only the mean NLL with this expression gives a number: trace .observation() .final_evaluation() .decoder() .mean_nll() trace.report() also states the evaluation unit, input identity, replay accounting and limits. It does not retrain a historical model or execute a seed sweep. structured evidence from this one observation; never parse stdout /// or run another model to produce either reporting projection. pub fn report(&self) -> Result<String, ReferenceHandoffError> { let run = &self.observation; let evaluation = run.final_evaluation(); let checkpoint = run.checkpoint(); let generation = run.generation(); let config = CapstoneConfig::tiny(); let targets_per_schedule = config.updates() * config.update_batch_size() * config.context_length(); let record = serde_json::json!({ "schema_version": 1, "chapter": "01-reference-core-handoff", "reference_identity": self.digest.as_hex(), "source_revision": self.source_revision, "scope": "scalar-reference-fixed-fixture-regression", "documents": { "train": run.partitions().train_document_ids().len(), "validation": run.partitions().validation_document_ids().len(), "test": run.partitions().test_document_ids().len() }, "model": { "parameters": run.training().parameter_count(), "context_tokens": config.context_length() }, "training": { "target_count_basis": "derived-from-frozen-full-batch-schedules", "updates_per_schedule": config.updates(), "independent_schedules": 2, "valid_targets_per_schedule": targets_per_schedule, "valid_targets_primary_plus_replay": 2 * targets_per_schedule, "selected_step": run.training().selected_step(), "within_invocation_replay_bitwise": run.training().replay_bitwise() }, "evaluation": { "unit": "overlapping-window-target-slot", "windows": evaluation.window_count(), "window_target_slots": evaluation.window_target_slot_count(), "document_transition_occurrences": evaluation.document_transition_occurrence_count(), "transition_multiplicity_counts": evaluation.transition_multiplicity_counts(), "decoder_mean_nll_nats_per_slot": evaluation.decoder().mean_nll(), "bigram_mean_nll_nats_per_slot": evaluation.bigram().mean_nll(), "once_per_transition_metric_reported": false, "independent_generalization_estimate": false }, "checkpoint": { "bytes_roundtrip": checkpoint.bytes_roundtrip(), "model_bits_exact": checkpoint.model_bits_exact(), "optimizer_bits_exact": checkpoint.optimizer_bits_exact(), "tokenizer_exact": checkpoint.tokenizer_exact(), "logit_probe_text": checkpoint.logit_probe_text(), "logit_probe_ids": checkpoint.logit_probe_ids(), "probe_logits_bitwise": checkpoint.prompt_logits_bitwise(), "complete_job_resume_established": false }, "generation": { "prompt": generation.prompt_text(), "token_ids": generation.generated_ids(), "decoded_text": generation.decoded_text(), "cached_reference_tokens_exact": generation.tokens_exact(), "cached_reference_decisions_bitwise": generation.decisions_bitwise(), "cached_reference_rng_exact": generation.rng_state_exact(), "useful_language_quality_established": false }, "laptop_throughput_measured": false, "successor_chapter": SUCCESSOR_CHAPTER }); let mut text = serde_json::to_string_pretty(&record) .map_err(|_| ReferenceHandoffError::Serialization)?; text.push('\n'); Ok(text) } Repeating seed 39 checks repeatability under fixed conditions. It does not estimate variability across seeds. Those are complementary checks, not interchangeable evidence. Run the reference without changing its inputs The example obtains verified source evidence and owns its temporary checkpoint location. Its report comes directly from the checked scalar observation, not from parsing a previous human-readable report. Verify the reference source, use an owned temporary checkpoint and print the scope-bearing report. rust/demos/practical-ch01-reference-core-handoff/src/main.rs#reference-example fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let source = verify_compiled_reference_source()?; let checkpoint = OwnedCheckpoint::new()?; let trace = run_reference_handoff(CORPUS, SPLITS, &checkpoint.file, &source)?; print!("{}", trace.report()?); Ok(()) } Keep the three evidence layers separate The digest identifies the fixed inputs. The counts and generated token IDs describe checked behavior on those inputs. The final card keeps future quality, job-resumption and hardware claims outside the reference’s evidence boundary. A reference identity is not a capability certificate The configuration, exact corpus and split bytes, and verified scalar-reference source determine the input identity. Separate checks observe replay, fixed-window evaluation, reload and cached generation. Neither the identity nor those checks establishes useful language quality, complete job resumption or laptop throughput. Identify the fixed inputs SHA-256 identity of the fixed input record 1ec769441b5ff648137bc5c381d2416045565986272b01dacafe8ac81f48fa01 Learned scalar parameters 1188 Read the checked reference behavior Overlapping test-window target slots 1744 Within-document transition occurrences 442 Generated token IDs [260,34,34] The target slots and transition occurrences belong to the same test documents. Each transition occurrence is one adjacent pair of token positions within a document. Overlapping windows score some occurrences more than once, giving more target slots than transition occurrences. Keep unmeasured capabilities separate Not established: useful language quality, complete job resumption or laptop throughput. Run the pure identity-input mutation test. Identify its changes to configuration, corpus, split bytes and source identity without training. Explain why constructing an identity for changed inputs does not admit them to the fixed reference run. From the repository root, with Docker and the Rust/site course image available, run: COURSE_CORPUS=false ./course run cargo test --offline --locked -p practical-ch01-reference-core-handoff --test reference_handoff every_identity_input_is_bound_without_training -- --exact Expected result: one selected test passes. A zero-test result does not reproduce this check. Explain why a successful checkpoint round trip cannot justify the statement “the complete training job can resume,” and why 1744 must not be labeled “distinct test transitions.” Answers: input identity, evidence scope and repeated target slots The digest binds inputs; replay and reload compare actual behavior. Neither kind of evidence substitutes for the other. The target-count basis explicitly derives 2048 targets per schedule and 4096 for primary plus replay. The reported mean NLL uses nats per overlapping window-target slot. The pure mutation test constructs different identities without calling the pipeline. The runner separately requires the exact accepted corpus and split bytes, so an identity is not an admission permit. The checkpoint check covers persisted model, optimizer and tokenizer state plus a fixed logit probe, not every whole-job continuation dependency. The 1744 denominator counts overlapping window-target slots; the underlying documents contain 442 transition occurrences. What the next extension must preserve You now have an identified scalar reference and a precisely bounded report. A later change can be compared with that reference, while carrying its own input identity and evidence. Chapter 2 uses NVIDIA NeMo Curator to prepare supplied text, then loads the prepared documents through the practical crate’s Rust reader. New data, larger models, accelerator execution, quality evaluation and complete job resumption each require their own checks; none is already established by this handoff. ← Previous chapter The structure of Practical LLM in Rust All chapters Next chapter → Prepare text externally, then load it in Rust

text: ← All chapters 02 · Content revision 1 Prepare text externally, then load it in Rust Use NVIDIA NeMo Curator to apply a word-count rule, remove repeated text and preserve known source-group splits, then load prepared JSONL in Rust. In this chapter Explain how source choices, exclusions, duplicates and evaluation overlap affect a training corpus; prepare a bounded example with NeMo Curator and load its selected documents through a caller-supplied Rust reader. Quick reference Corpus preparation Terms for selecting training text, handling repeated examples, protecting evaluation roles and reading prepared documents. Decontamination Check and exclude training overlap with declared protected evaluation material using a specified method. Passing that check does not establish absence of every possible leak. Document occurrence One stored instance of a document. Two records containing the same text are two occurrences and can give that text extra training weight. Exact deduplication Remove repeated text under a declared equality policy. The NeMo example groups text hashes and keeps one representative; it does not detect paraphrases or certify collision-proof equality. Held-out split Validation or test documents kept out of tokenizer learning and model fitting. Validation informs setting choices; test evaluation is reserved for the final assessment. Near-duplicate A document sufficiently similar to another under a declared matching method. Approximate searches can miss related text or group text that should remain distinct. Prepared-document interchange UTF-8 JSONL records with nonblank string id and text fields and retained metadata. Rust loads the supplied selection without redoing filtering, duplicate removal or split assignment. Retention fraction Prepared-document count divided by input-document count for a nonempty input. It measures how much the declared pipeline retains, not the quality of its survivors. Source group Records declared to belong to one related source family. The exercise assigns each supplied group to a single split; that assignment does not prove all related records were discovered. Training corpus The selected documents that supply examples for tokenizer learning and model training, together with evidence of their source and preparation policy. The problem: the model learns from the text we let through A language model learns to predict tokens from the documents supplied during training. Its optimizer does not decide whether those documents are appropriate for the task, whether we may use them, or whether a purportedly unseen test example also appears in the training input. Those decisions must happen before training. Repeated text creates another problem. If one training pass visits every stored document occurrence, each copy of a document supplies another copy of its token targets. The repeated text receives more influence without adding new examples. Removing duplicates changes that weighting; it does not merely save disk space. Corpus preparation therefore has two outputs: selected text and evidence about how it was selected. We need source context, declared exclusion rules, duplicate handling and protected evaluation boundaries. A large file or a successful download supplies none of those conclusions on its own. We will use NVIDIA NeMo Curator to prepare text. It is an external tool, not part of the Rust language model, and another preparation tool can replace it if it produces the same documented input for the model. Rust will only load the prepared documents. The extended tokenizer in Chapter 3 will then learn from the training documents, not the validation or test documents. The solution: prepare documents, then load a stable format Keep one document as one record throughout the preparation pipeline. Retain a stable document ID and the source information needed to trace that record. A source record should identify where the text came from, its revision and the applicable license and attribution. A checksum identifies selected bytes; it does not establish permission to use those bytes or tell us what they contain. Apply declared quality rules, inspect what those rules exclude, and handle duplicates before final training input is frozen. Quality rules are proxies: for example, a minimum word count rejects short records, not every unsuitable record. A rule can also remove useful text. Inspect both survivors and exclusions rather than interpreting a low exclusion rate as success. Keep privacy review separate from quality scoring. Passing a word-count filter or removing duplicates does not remove names, addresses, credentials or other sensitive content. Withhold unresolved records from training; do not copy their sensitive text into public reports. Retain enough source and transformation information to identify affected derived corpora if an input is withdrawn. Removing a source from a later corpus does not erase what an already trained model may have learned from it. A six-document example The practical example uses course-authored text, not a result for a large training corpus. Its JSONL input contains these six documents: Document ID | Text | Source group | Relevant observation story-a | A cat naps. | family-a | Three words story-b | A cat naps. | family-a | An identical copy of story-a story-c | A dog runs. | family-b | Three words story-d | Rain feeds trees. | family-c | Three words story-e | hi | family-e | One word story-f | !!! | family-f | Punctuation only Configure NeMo’s word-count filter to retain records with at least 3 and at most 20 words. Its English setting counts whitespace-separated items; that proxy is not a linguistic definition of a word. The 4 story occurrences survive; hi and the punctuation-only record do not. Exact duplicate removal then leaves 3 distinct story texts. The punctuation-only record has one whitespace-separated item too; this particular rule rejects it for length, not because it recognizes punctuation as unsuitable language-model training text. The duplicate-removal workflow may retain either cat-story ID; the result we care about here is one cat-story occurrence, not a promised representative ID or output-file order. Before deduplication, the cat story occupies 2 of the 4 surviving document occurrences. After deduplication, it occupies 1 of 3 distinct documents. Under uniform sampling of these whole-stage document occurrences before separating their roles, its selection probability would change from 2/4 to 1/3. That calculation illustrates duplicate weighting, not a sampler used to train on this fixture. Actual token-target weighting also depends on document length, split selection and the batching policy; document fractions are not token fractions. NeMo’s exact method groups hashes of text and identifies copies to remove. It does not identify paraphrases, and hash grouping is not an adversarial collision-proof comparison. NeMo’s fuzzy method uses approximate similarity search for near-duplicates. Its configuration trades missed matches against unwanted matches; it does not certify a universal similarity cutoff or detect all ways an evaluation example could have leaked into training. Freeze the roles of the prepared documents The training split supplies examples for fitting the tokenizer and model. The validation split supplies examples for selecting settings or deciding when to stop training. The test split is reserved for final evaluation. Do not move a difficult held-out document into training after seeing its score. Related records must not be scattered across those roles. Treat an identified duplicate family or other known related source group as one unit when assigning splits. Otherwise two different IDs can put substantially the same example in both training and evaluation. For this fixture, the two cat-story copies share family-a; their different IDs do not make them independent examples. For the exercise, a supplied policy assigns family-a, family-e and family-f to training, family-b to validation and family-c to test. We fix that policy before running the filters. Both cat-story copies therefore have the same role regardless of which ID duplicate removal keeps. The prepared fixture has one document in each role: the cat story in training, the dog story in validation and the rain story in test. The recipe uses Pandas to join those declared assignments to the source-group metadata. It refuses an unassigned group rather than choosing a convenient role after seeing the output. This checks the supplied groups, not whether we have discovered every related pair. One held-out story is also far too little evidence for a meaningful model-quality estimate. Split disjointness and decontamination are different checks. Disjoint IDs do not prove different text. Removing exact duplicates does not prove that near-copies or external benchmark examples are absent. Declare the protected evaluation material and the overlap method before inspecting results, report its measured scope, and keep unresolved overlaps out of training. A check against a named evaluation set does not establish internet-wide contamination freedom. Export documents, not preparation-specific objects The handoff to Rust is UTF-8 JSON Lines: one JSON object per physical line. Each object has a nonblank string id and a nonblank string text. Other fields are retained as metadata. For example: {"id":"story-c","text":"A dog runs.","source_group":"family-b"} The document ID is a label, not a token ID or a required filename. The text is still text; tokenization comes next. A newline inside document text must be escaped as \n inside the JSON string, so it does not create a second record. Source and split records remain linked to the exported documents, but a JSONL file alone does not certify that those decisions were made correctly. Formula: distinguish retention from quality For a nonempty input corpus, the final document-retention fraction is r_{\mathrm{keep}}=\frac{N_{\mathrm{prepared}}}{N_{\mathrm{input}}} Here N_{\mathrm{input}} is the number of input document occurrences, N_{\mathrm{prepared}} is the number remaining after the declared preparation stages, and r_{\mathrm{keep}} is a dimensionless fraction. Neither count is a byte count or token count. With zero input documents, the fraction is undefined; report that condition rather than inventing a zero-quality score. In the six-document example, quality filtering retains 4/6 of the original input. Duplicate removal retains 3/4 of its own input: the four records that reached that stage. Their product is the final retention fraction, \frac{4}{6}\cdot\frac{3}{4}=\frac{3}{6}=\frac{1}{2}. Changing the denominator changes the question. Reporting 1/6 as the duplicate stage’s exclusion fraction would use the original input population rather than the 4 records the duplicate stage examined. Keep every stage’s entering and leaving document counts so its fraction can be interpreted locally. Keeping half the input says how much remains under this policy. It does not say that half was bad, that the survivors are safe, or that a model trained on them will perform well. Those claims need different evidence. Practical preparation with NeMo Curator This workflow uses a separately built NeMo Curator image. You need Linux, Docker, a compatible NVIDIA GPU and driver, and the NVIDIA Container Toolkit so Docker can expose the GPU. The pinned NeMo release must be compatible with that CUDA/driver stack. Rust’s prepared-corpus reader does not require a GPU or CUDA. Run the following commands from the repository root. The image build may use network access to obtain the external tool. It does not acquire a training corpus or add NeMo to the Rust/site image: docker build --file docker/nemo-curator.Dockerfile \ --tag learn-llm-nemo-curator:26.07 . With the NeMo image built and the NVIDIA GPU available to Docker, run from the repository root. Create a fresh output directory for the exercise, then run the tool with network access disabled. The read-only mount supplies the recipe and its six-record fixture; the writable mount receives generated preparation output: mkdir -p .build/corpus/practical-ch02-exact-fixture docker run --rm --network none --gpus all --memory=8g --cpus=2 --shm-size=1g \ --hostname course-nemo --add-host course-nemo:127.0.0.1 \ --mount type=bind,source="$PWD/tools/nemo-curator",target=/course,readonly \ --mount type=bind,source="$PWD/.build/corpus/practical-ch02-exact-fixture",target=/output \ learn-llm-nemo-curator:26.07 \ /course/prepare_corpus.py \ --input /course/fixtures/raw.jsonl --output /output \ --split-policy /course/fixtures/splits.json Use an empty output directory. If the directory already contains an earlier attempt, choose a different directory rather than overwriting its evidence. The hostname mapping lets the local Ray workers resolve their container on loopback; it does not enable external network access. The recipe invokes NeMo’s reader, configured word-count filter, exact duplicate identification and duplicate-removal workflow. Identification produces IDs to remove; it is not already the prepared text. The removal workflow must consume those IDs from the same input and ID policy, then export the remaining documents. The filter configuration in tools/nemo-curator/prepare_corpus.py uses the library’s pipeline and stages; the recipe does not implement its own filter: Pipeline( name="course_corpus_quality", stages=[ JsonlReader(file_paths=str(input_path), read_kwargs=read_kwargs), ScoreFilter( filter_obj=WordCountFilter(min_words=min_words, max_words=max_words, lang="en"), score_field="word_count", ), JsonlWriter(path=str(quality_path), mode="error"), ], ).run(executor=executor) The surrounding recipe supplies the reader settings, starts a local Ray client, and runs NeMo’s exact-identification and text-removal workflows. The defaults set min_words to 3 and max_words to 20. Command-line options change those values; retain them with the output report when comparing different policies. The supplied split-policy file is independent of the observed scores. Inspect the generated report and exported files with these commands, still from the repository root: cat .build/corpus/practical-ch02-exact-fixture/report.json cat .build/corpus/practical-ch02-exact-fixture/prepared.jsonl cat .build/corpus/practical-ch02-exact-fixture/train.jsonl For this fixture, the expected stage counts are 6 input documents, 4 after word-count filtering and 3 after exact duplicate removal. The final texts are A cat naps., A dog runs. and Rain feeds trees.; do not require one particular cat-story ID. The report also records one document in each role. prepared.jsonl contains all three documents for inspection; train.jsonl, validation.jsonl and test.jsonl contain their respective selections and retain the split metadata. This is a tiny execution example with a fixed assignment of known source groups. It is not an approval of a larger corpus, a privacy check, proof that all related groups were found or a trained-model result. The helper limits input to 4 MiB and 4096 documents by default so the example is inspectable; those are not a recipe for processing the previously acquired large corpus. A bulk run needs its own feasible configuration and complete selection evidence. For a real corpus, also retain input provenance, the tool version and configuration, excluded-document counts, the duplicate policy, split assignments and the scope of overlap and privacy review. A successful small fixture does not establish that the same resource settings fit a larger dataset. Select and measure that workload separately, preserving the raw inputs and every failed attempt. Load the prepared output in Rust PreparedCorpusReader accepts any caller-supplied BufRead stream. A file, memory buffer or database export can supply that stream without changing the loader. Standard buffered I/O reads physical lines; Serde JSON parses their objects. The loader preserves decoded text and metadata. It does not normalize text, reject duplicate content or assign a split. The prepared-corpus loader uses Serde JSON to decode required document fields, then rejects blank IDs or text without rewriting their content. rust/crates/llm-from-scratch-practical/src/data/prepared_corpus.rs#prepared-document-json let document: PreparedDocument = serde_json::from_slice(&self.buffer) .map_err(|source| CorpusReadError::InvalidJson { line, source })?; for (field, value) in [("id", &document.id), ("text", &document.text)] { if value.trim().is_empty() { return Err(CorpusReadError::EmptyField { line, field }); } } The caller chooses maximum source-record bytes, document count and cumulative decoded-text bytes. Record bytes include the physical line ending; decoded text bytes count the UTF-8 representation of the text value, not JSON syntax or metadata. An oversized record, malformed JSON, missing required field, failed read or exceeded limit stops the stream with an error. No failed document is returned or counted. Documents returned earlier are not rolled back. The prepared-corpus iterator stops after successful end of input or its first error; it never resumes past a failed record. rust/crates/llm-from-scratch-practical/src/data/prepared_corpus.rs#prepared-corpus-stream fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item> { if self.finished { return None; } match self.read_document() { Ok(Some(document)) => Some(Ok(document)), Ok(None) => { self.finished = true; None } Err(error) => { self.finished = true; Some(Err(error)) } } } The demo reads standard input, retains only the first three document descriptions for its summary, and emits that summary only after the complete input succeeds. It can therefore inspect a large stream without retaining every text. This is not a transactional storage adapter: a caller storing documents as they arrive must provide its own staging if partial results must stay unpublished. The Rust demo loads supplied prepared documents, reports their count and decoded text bytes, and does not repeat NeMo's preparation operations. rust/demos/practical-ch02-corpus-preparation/src/lib.rs#load-prepared-corpus pub fn summarize<R: BufRead>( source: R, limits: ReadLimits, ) -> Result<CorpusSummary, CorpusReadError> { let mut documents = PreparedCorpusReader::new(source, limits)?; let mut first_documents = Vec::with_capacity(SUMMARY_DOCUMENTS); for document in documents.by_ref() { let document = document?; if first_documents.len() < SUMMARY_DOCUMENTS { first_documents.push(DocumentSummary { id: document.id, metadata_fields: document.metadata.keys().cloned().collect(), text_utf8_bytes: document.text.len(), }); } // The tokenizer can consume document.text here. This chapter only loads // prepared records; no preparation operation is repeated inside Rust. } Ok(CorpusSummary { first_documents, loaded: documents.progress(), }) } With Docker running and the Rust workspace image available, load the output from the preceding NeMo command. Run from the repository root: COURSE_CORPUS=false ./course run cargo run --offline --locked \ -p practical-ch02-corpus-preparation \ < .build/corpus/practical-ch02-exact-fixture/prepared.jsonl The Rust summary should report 3 loaded documents and 39 decoded text bytes. Those bytes are 11 for the cat story, 11 for the dog story and 17 for the rain story. Metadata and JSON punctuation are not included in that sum. The wrapper runs the Rust program without network access; COURSE_CORPUS=false avoids acquiring the optional large corpus while preparing the Rust image. With Docker running and the Rust workspace image available, run from the repository root. For the tokenizer’s training input, select the training export created by the NeMo command instead of the all-role inspection file: COURSE_CORPUS=false ./course run cargo run --offline --locked \ -p practical-ch02-corpus-preparation \ < .build/corpus/practical-ch02-exact-fixture/train.jsonl This summary reports 1 document and 11 decoded text bytes. Choosing that file is the caller’s responsibility: the loader does not infer a role from a filename or reject held-out records automatically. The executable receives a corpus through standard input and prints its summary only after the reader reaches successful end of input. rust/demos/practical-ch02-corpus-preparation/src/main.rs#prepared-corpus-example fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> { // stdin is supplied by the caller: a file redirect, pipe, or other source. // No HTTP, asset path, dataset choice, or GPU is built into this executable. let report = summarize(std::io::stdin().lock(), DEMO_LIMITS)?; println!("{}", serde_json::to_string_pretty(&report)?); Ok(()) } History: more text was not the whole solution Collecting readable text alone does not document its intended use, control the weight of repeated occurrences or protect held-out evaluation from training overlap. Dataset documentation makes source context reviewable; deduplication studies connect repeated training text with memorization and train-test overlap in their measured settings. Datasheets for Datasets was first posted in 2018. Gebru and colleagues propose documenting dataset motivation, composition, collection and intended uses so those choices can be reviewed. Documentation records context; it does not itself establish permission or privacy. The 2021 C4 analysis examined where web-corpus text came from and what filtering removed. Its finding that blocklist filtering disproportionately excluded text from and about minority individuals is a reason to inspect exclusions, not to label every filter neutral. In 2022, Deduplicating Training Data Makes Language Models Better studied duplicate handling in training corpora. Lee and colleagues report reduced memorized output and train-test overlap after deduplication in their studied corpora and models; those outcomes are not measurements of this course fixture. They explain why duplicate handling and evaluation separation matter in addition to collecting and documenting text. The following Rust comparison loads two identical supplied records and keeps both. It illustrates the limitation of merely reading raw occurrences, not a reimplementation of those studies’ preparation tools: Reading two identical JSONL records returns two documents; the loader does not silently perform duplicate removal. rust/crates/llm-from-scratch-practical/src/data/prepared_corpus.rs#loading-is-not-preparation #[test] fn loader_does_not_curate_repeated_ids_or_text() { let source = b"{\"id\":\"same\",\"text\":\"same text\"}\n{\"id\":\"same\",\"text\":\"same text\"}\n"; let documents = PreparedCorpusReader::new(Cursor::new(source), limits()) .unwrap() .collect::<Result<Vec<_>, _>>() .unwrap(); assert_eq!(documents.len(), 2); assert_eq!(documents[0], documents[1]); } Keep documented source and selection evidence, inspect exclusions, handle related records together and preserve held-out roles before tokenizer learning or model training. No single preparation statistic certifies suitability. Follow the preparation-to-learning boundary Prepare documents outside the Rust language model The six-document course fixture passes through NeMo's word-count rule and exact duplicate removal, leaving three documents. A fixed policy assigns known source groups to training, validation and test; Rust loads the exported records. Document counts count those records. Decoded text bytes measure only the UTF-8 size of their text, excluding metadata. Neither quantity certifies privacy, complete related-source discovery or trained-model quality. 1. Declare the source and policy Keep document IDs, source-group metadata and intended-use context. Freeze quality and split choices before observing their outcomes. Fixture input documents 6 2. Run external NeMo preparation After the word-count rule 4 document occurrences After exact duplicate removal 3 documents Final document-retention fraction \frac{3}{6} The fraction divides the final prepared count by the original input count of 6 documents. One cat-story occurrence remains. Either original cat-story ID may be kept. 3. Export and load the selected role NeMo-prepared JSONL crosses into a caller-supplied Rust reader. Loading validates records and limits, not their suitability for training. All-role inspection export loaded by Rust 3 documents; 39 decoded text bytes Training export loaded by Rust 1 document; 11 decoded text bytes The provided groups keep the three learning roles separate Training 1 fixture document; 11 decoded text bytes. Learn tokenizer choices and fit the model. Validation 1 fixture document; 11 decoded text bytes. Select settings; do not learn tokenizer choices from this text. Quick reference Corpus preparation Terms for selecting training text, handling repeated examples, protecting evaluation roles and reading prepared documents. Decontamination Check and exclude training overlap with declared protected evaluation material using a specified method. Passing that check does not establish absence of every possible leak. Document occurrence One stored instance of a document. Two records containing the same text are two occurrences and can give that text extra training weight. Exact deduplication Remove repeated text under a declared equality policy. The NeMo example groups text hashes and keeps one representative; it does not detect paraphrases or certify collision-proof equality. Held-out split Validation or test documents kept out of tokenizer learning and model fitting. Validation informs setting choices; test evaluation is reserved for the final assessment. Near-duplicate A document sufficiently similar to another under a declared matching method. Approximate searches can miss related text or group text that should remain distinct. Prepared-document interchange UTF-8 JSONL records with nonblank string id and text fields and retained metadata. Rust loads the supplied selection without redoing filtering, duplicate removal or split assignment. Retention fraction Prepared-document count divided by input-document count for a nonempty input. It measures how much the declared pipeline retains, not the quality of its survivors. Source group Records declared to belong to one related source family. The exercise assigns each supplied group to a single split; that assignment does not prove all related records were discovered. Training corpus The selected documents that supply examples for tokenizer learning and model training, together with evidence of their source and preparation policy. The problem: the model learns from the text we let through A language model learns to predict tokens from the documents supplied during training. Its optimizer does not decide whether those documents are appropriate for the task, whether we may use them, or whether a purportedly unseen test example also appears in the training input. Those decisions must happen before training. Repeated text creates another problem. If one training pass visits every stored document occurrence, each copy of a document supplies another copy of its token targets. The repeated text receives more influence without adding new examples. Removing duplicates changes that weighting; it does not merely save disk space. Corpus preparation therefore has two outputs: selected text and evidence about how it was selected. We need source context, declared exclusion rules, duplicate handling and protected evaluation boundaries. A large file or a successful download supplies none of those conclusions on its own. We will use NVIDIA NeMo Curator to prepare text. It is an external tool, not part of the Rust language model, and another preparation tool can replace it if it produces the same documented input for the model. Rust will only load the prepared documents. The extended tokenizer in Chapter 3 will then learn from the training documents, not the validation or test documents. The solution: prepare documents, then load a stable format Keep one document as one record throughout the preparation pipeline. Retain a stable document ID and the source information needed to trace that record. A source record should identify where the text came from, its revision and the applicable license and attribution. A checksum identifies selected bytes; it does not establish permission to use those bytes or tell us what they contain. Apply declared quality rules, inspect what those rules exclude, and handle duplicates before final training input is frozen. Quality rules are proxies: for example, a minimum word count rejects short records, not every unsuitable record. A rule can also remove useful text. Inspect both survivors and exclusions rather than interpreting a low exclusion rate as success. Keep privacy review separate from quality scoring. Passing a word-count filter or removing duplicates does not remove names, addresses, credentials or other sensitive content. Withhold unresolved records from training; do not copy their sensitive text into public reports. Retain enough source and transformation information to identify affected derived corpora if an input is withdrawn. Removing a source from a later corpus does not erase what an already trained model may have learned from it. A six-document example The practical example uses course-authored text, not a result for a large training corpus. Its JSONL input contains these six documents: Document ID | Text | Source group | Relevant observation story-a | A cat naps. | family-a | Three words story-b | A cat naps. | family-a | An identical copy of story-a story-c | A dog runs. | family-b | Three words story-d | Rain feeds trees. | family-c | Three words story-e | hi | family-e | One word story-f | !!! | family-f | Punctuation only Configure NeMo’s word-count filter to retain records with at least 3 and at most 20 words. Its English setting counts whitespace-separated items; that proxy is not a linguistic definition of a word. The 4 story occurrences survive; hi and the punctuation-only record do not. Exact duplicate removal then leaves 3 distinct story texts. The punctuation-only record has one whitespace-separated item too; this particular rule rejects it for length, not because it recognizes punctuation as unsuitable language-model training text. The duplicate-removal workflow may retain either cat-story ID; the result we care about here is one cat-story occurrence, not a promised representative ID or output-file order. Before deduplication, the cat story occupies 2 of the 4 surviving document occurrences. After deduplication, it occupies 1 of 3 distinct documents. Under uniform sampling of these whole-stage document occurrences before separating their roles, its selection probability would change from 2/4 to 1/3. That calculation illustrates duplicate weighting, not a sampler used to train on this fixture. Actual token-target weighting also depends on document length, split selection and the batching policy; document fractions are not token fractions. NeMo’s exact method groups hashes of text and identifies copies to remove. It does not identify paraphrases, and hash grouping is not an adversarial collision-proof comparison. NeMo’s fuzzy method uses approximate similarity search for near-duplicates. Its configuration trades missed matches against unwanted matches; it does not certify a universal similarity cutoff or detect all ways an evaluation example could have leaked into training. Freeze the roles of the prepared documents The training split supplies examples for fitting the tokenizer and model. The validation split supplies examples for selecting settings or deciding when to stop training. The test split is reserved for final evaluation. Do not move a difficult held-out document into training after seeing its score. Related records must not be scattered across those roles. Treat an identified duplicate family or other known related source group as one unit when assigning splits. Otherwise two different IDs can put substantially the same example in both training and evaluation. For this fixture, the two cat-story copies share family-a; their different IDs do not make them independent examples. For the exercise, a supplied policy assigns family-a, family-e and family-f to training, family-b to validation and family-c to test. We fix that policy before running the filters. Both cat-story copies therefore have the same role regardless of which ID duplicate removal keeps. The prepared fixture has one document in each role: the cat story in training, the dog story in validation and the rain story in test. The recipe uses Pandas to join those declared assignments to the source-group metadata. It refuses an unassigned group rather than choosing a convenient role after seeing the output. This checks the supplied groups, not whether we have discovered every related pair. One held-out story is also far too little evidence for a meaningful model-quality estimate. Split disjointness and decontamination are different checks. Disjoint IDs do not prove different text. Removing exact duplicates does not prove that near-copies or external benchmark examples are absent. Declare the protected evaluation material and the overlap method before inspecting results, report its measured scope, and keep unresolved overlaps out of training. A check against a named evaluation set does not establish internet-wide contamination freedom. Export documents, not preparation-specific objects The handoff to Rust is UTF-8 JSON Lines: one JSON object per physical line. Each object has a nonblank string id and a nonblank string text. Other fields are retained as metadata. For example: {"id":"story-c","text":"A dog runs.","source_group":"family-b"} The document ID is a label, not a token ID or a required filename. The text is still text; tokenization comes next. A newline inside document text must be escaped as \n inside the JSON string, so it does not create a second record. Source and split records remain linked to the exported documents, but a JSONL file alone does not certify that those decisions were made correctly. Formula: distinguish retention from quality For a nonempty input corpus, the final document-retention fraction is r_{\mathrm{keep}}=\frac{N_{\mathrm{prepared}}}{N_{\mathrm{input}}} Here N_{\mathrm{input}} is the number of input document occurrences, N_{\mathrm{prepared}} is the number remaining after the declared preparation stages, and r_{\mathrm{keep}} is a dimensionless fraction. Neither count is a byte count or token count. With zero input documents, the fraction is undefined; report that condition rather than inventing a zero-quality score. In the six-document example, quality filtering retains 4/6 of the original input. Duplicate removal retains 3/4 of its own input: the four records that reached that stage. Their product is the final retention fraction, \frac{4}{6}\cdot\frac{3}{4}=\frac{3}{6}=\frac{1}{2}. Changing the denominator changes the question. Reporting 1/6 as the duplicate stage’s exclusion fraction would use the original input population rather than the 4 records the duplicate stage examined. Keep every stage’s entering and leaving document counts so its fraction can be interpreted locally. Keeping half the input says how much remains under this policy. It does not say that half was bad, that the survivors are safe, or that a model trained on them will perform well. Those claims need different evidence. Practical preparation with NeMo Curator This workflow uses a separately built NeMo Curator image. You need Linux, Docker, a compatible NVIDIA GPU and driver, and the NVIDIA Container Toolkit so Docker can expose the GPU. The pinned NeMo release must be compatible with that CUDA/driver stack. Rust’s prepared-corpus reader does not require a GPU or CUDA. Run the following commands from the repository root. The image build may use network access to obtain the external tool. It does not acquire a training corpus or add NeMo to the Rust/site image: docker build --file docker/nemo-curator.Dockerfile \ --tag learn-llm-nemo-curator:26.07 . With the NeMo image built and the NVIDIA GPU available to Docker, run from the repository root. Create a fresh output directory for the exercise, then run the tool with network access disabled. The read-only mount supplies the recipe and its six-record fixture; the writable mount receives generated preparation output: mkdir -p .build/corpus/practical-ch02-exact-fixture docker run --rm --network none --gpus all --memory=8g --cpus=2 --shm-size=1g \ --hostname course-nemo --add-host course-nemo:127.0.0.1 \ --mount type=bind,source="$PWD/tools/nemo-curator",target=/course,readonly \ --mount type=bind,source="$PWD/.build/corpus/practical-ch02-exact-fixture",target=/output \ learn-llm-nemo-curator:26.07 \ /course/prepare_corpus.py \ --input /course/fixtures/raw.jsonl --output /output \ --split-policy /course/fixtures/splits.json Use an empty output directory.
